1: The realm of the dead in the Hebrew Bible: a shadowy, silent place 'down' beneath the earth where all the dead go, righteous and wicked alike. Its etymology is uncertain (proposals include a link to sha'al, 'to ask', or to a root meaning 'hollow'). It is not, in most texts, a place of punishment; it is the common destination of mortals, characterised by silence, darkness and separation from the worship of God.
2: About 65-66 occurrences in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in Psalms, Job, Proverbs and Isaiah. The KJV renders it inconsistently as 'grave' (31 times), 'hell' (31 times) and 'pit' (3 times), which has caused much confusion; most modern versions transliterate it as Sheol. Jacob expects to go down to Sheol mourning (Gen 37:35); Job longs to hide there (Job 14:13); the Psalms lament that no one praises God there (Ps 6:5, Ps 88:10-12), yet also confess that God is present even in Sheol (Ps 139:8) and can redeem from it (Ps 49:15). Isaiah 14 pictures its shades rousing to greet the fallen king of Babylon. The Septuagint usually translates it with hades.
4: Sheol reflects an early Israelite view shared with the ancient Near East: a gloomy, undifferentiated underworld with no clear hope of reward or punishment. Hope beyond death develops late, in texts such as Isa 26:19 and Dan 12:2.
6: Sheol is the place or state of the dead before Christ. Many Fathers and later Protestant interpreters held that it had compartments for righteous and wicked, read in light of Luke 16; texts such as Ps 16:10 and Ps 49:15 already hint at deliverance from it.
8: Sheol is essentially 'the grave' or the condition of death itself: the dead are unconscious and await resurrection. Passages about silence in Sheol (Eccl 9:10, Ps 6:5) are read literally.
10: Later Jewish tradition developed Sheol into Gehinnom (a place of purification or punishment, usually temporary) and Gan Eden (the garden for the righteous), while retaining belief in resurrection (techiyat ha-metim).
12: In Greek religion the god of the underworld and then the underworld itself. In the Septuagint it translates Sheol, and in the New Testament it denotes the realm of the dead, personified alongside Death as an enemy that Christ overcomes. It is distinct from Gehenna: Hades holds the dead until the resurrection and is itself emptied and destroyed at the end (Rev 20:13-14).
13: Ten occurrences in the critical Greek New Testament (an eleventh at 1 Cor 15:55 in the Textus Receptus): Matt 11:23, Matt 16:18, Luke 10:15, Luke 16:23, Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31, Rev 1:18, Rev 6:8, Rev 20:13, Rev 20:14. The KJV renders all as 'hell', which blurs the Hades/Gehenna distinction. Acts 2 applies Ps 16:10 to Jesus, who was not abandoned to Hades. Luke 16:23 is the only text that pictures conscious torment in Hades.
15: Hades is the interim realm of the dead before the final judgment. Luke 16 shows that the dead are conscious and already experience either comfort or distress before the resurrection.
17: Luke 16:19-31 is a parable that uses popular Jewish imagery to make a point about wealth and repentance; it should not be pressed for a map of the afterlife. Hades elsewhere simply means death's domain.
19: Christ holds the keys of Death and Hades (Rev 1:18) because he entered the realm of the dead and broke its power; the gates of Hades cannot prevail against the church (Matt 16:18). Eastern iconography of the Anastasis pictures Christ pulling Adam and Eve from Hades.
21: Hades equals the grave, the state of being dead. The personification of Hades with Death in Revelation supports reading it as a power of death, not a place of conscious souls.
23: Named after the valley south and southwest of Jerusalem where, according to the prophets, children were burned in sacrifice (2 Kgs 23:10, Jer 7:31-32). Jeremiah announced it would become a 'valley of slaughter'. By the Second Temple period (1 Enoch 26-27 already describes an accursed valley beside Jerusalem as a place of judgment) the name had become a term for the place of final judgment of the wicked. In the New Testament it is the place of post-judgment punishment, where both body and soul can be destroyed (Matt 10:28).
24: Twelve occurrences: eleven on the lips of Jesus in the Synoptic Gospels (Matt 5:22, Matt 5:29, Matt 5:30, Matt 10:28, Matt 18:9, Matt 23:15, Matt 23:33, Mark 9:43, Mark 9:45, Mark 9:47, Luke 12:5) and once in James (Jas 3:6). Mark 9:48 quotes Isa 66:24 on the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched. The popular claim that the valley was a perpetually burning city rubbish dump is first attested in medieval Jewish commentary (often traced to David Kimhi, c. 1200) and is doubted by many scholars.
26: Gehenna is the final hell where the wicked suffer unending conscious torment; unquenchable fire and undying worm signal endless duration, and Matt 25:46 pairs eternal punishment with eternal life.
28: Isa 66:24 depicts corpses, not living sufferers; 'destroy both soul and body in Gehenna' (Matt 10:28) points to final extinction. The fire is unquenchable in that it cannot be put out until it has consumed, not that its victims live forever.
30: Gehenna is real and fearful but remedial: a purging fire whose purpose is correction. Its fire is God's own consuming love, and its result is restoration, not endless loss.
32: Some interpreters read Jesus' Gehenna warnings, at least partly, as prophetic threats about the coming destruction of Jerusalem (AD 70), when the valley would again be filled with corpses, echoing Jeremiah.
34: In Greek mythology Tartarus was the deepest pit beneath Hades where the Titans were imprisoned. The New Testament uses the verb once, of God consigning sinning angels to chains of darkness until judgment. Hellenistic Jewish writings (e.g. 1 Enoch 20:2 in the Greek) also used Tartarus for the prison of rebel angels.
35: One occurrence (2 Pet 2:4), a verb. Jude 1:6 describes the same tradition without the word. The background is the Watchers tradition of Gen 6:1-4 developed in 1 Enoch.
37: Tartarus is a specific holding place for fallen angels (distinct from Hades for humans), reflecting 1 Enoch's Watchers tradition, which Peter and Jude assume.
39: Many older commentators treat Tartarus simply as a synonym for hell, the place of punishment for fallen angels and the wicked.
41: Peter borrows a familiar Greek term to communicate with Hellenistic readers; the point is the certainty of judgment, not cosmological detail.
43: Revelation's image for the final destination of the beast, false prophet, devil, Death, Hades, and those not found in the book of life. It is explicitly identified with 'the second death'. Fire-and-brimstone imagery recalls Sodom (Gen 19:24) and prophetic judgment oracles.
44: Found only in Revelation 19-21 (Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14, Rev 20:15, Rev 21:8). The beast and false prophet are thrown in first (19:20), then the devil, who is tormented 'day and night for ever and ever' (20:10). Death and Hades are thrown in (20:14). Jesus' phrase 'eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels' (Matt 25:41) is usually connected.
45: Rev 20:10 states that the devil, beast and false prophet are tormented forever; humans who share their fate (20:15, compare Rev 14:10-11) share their unending torment.
47: The lake is 'the second death'. Death and Hades, which are not persons, are thrown in and abolished, which suggests destruction; the torment of 20:10 is said of the beast and false prophet, symbolic figures for empires and systems.
49: Fire and brimstone (theion, associated with divine purification) point to purification. The gates of the New Jerusalem are never shut (Rev 21:25) and the nations are healed (Rev 22:2), hinting that the lake is not the last word.
51: As apocalyptic imagery, the lake communicates total and final defeat of evil; questions of duration and consciousness must be settled from other texts, not from the image alone.
53: The primeval deep (Gen 1:2, where the Septuagint has abyssos) and, in later usage, the underworld prison of demonic powers. In Romans it stands for the realm of the dead.
54: Nine occurrences in the New Testament: Luke 8:31 (the demons beg not to be sent there), Rom 10:7 (who will descend into the abyss, i.e. to bring Christ up from the dead), and seven in Revelation (Rev 9:1, Rev 9:2, Rev 9:11, Rev 11:7, Rev 17:8, Rev 20:1, Rev 20:3), where it is a shaft with a key, the source of the beast, and the place where Satan is bound for a thousand years.
56: The abyss is a real holding place for evil spirits, distinct from the lake of fire, from which Satan is released before final judgment.
58: The abyss echoes ancient Near Eastern chaos waters (tehom); evil rising from it is the return of uncreation, which God subdues as he did at creation.
60: Satan's binding in the abyss describes the present church age, in which he cannot deceive the nations so as to stop the gospel (compare Matt 12:29).
62: The binding is a future event after Christ's return, ushering in a literal thousand-year reign on earth.
64: A royal park or garden. The Septuagint used paradeisos for the garden of Eden (Gen 2:8). In Second Temple Judaism it came to denote the abode of the righteous dead and the restored Eden of the end time.
65: Pardes occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible (Neh 2:8, Eccl 2:5, Song 4:13), always of ordinary parks or orchards. Paradeisos occurs three times in the New Testament: Jesus' promise to the penitent thief (Luke 23:43), Paul caught up to Paradise, identified with the third heaven (2 Cor 12:2-4), and the tree of life in the paradise of God (Rev 2:7).
67: Paradise is where the righteous go immediately at death to be with Christ (Luke 23:43, compare Phil 1:23), awaiting the resurrection.
69: Some read Luke 23:43 as 'I tell you today, you will be with me in Paradise', placing the promise at the resurrection. Most grammarians and translators reject this, since 'Truly I tell you' is a fixed formula in Luke without 'today'.
71: Paradise is primarily eschatological: the renewed creation in which humanity regains access to the tree of life (Rev 2:7, Rev 22:2). Its use for the intermediate state is an anticipation of this.
73: Some Fathers and later dispensational writers held that Paradise (Abraham's bosom) was a section of Hades until Christ's ascension, when it was moved up to heaven (with appeal to Eph 4:8-10).
75: A place of honour and comfort beside Abraham, as at a banquet where the favoured guest reclines next to the host (compare John 13:23). In Jewish usage it expressed the destiny of the righteous dead (compare 4 Maccabees 13:17, where the patriarchs receive the martyrs).
76: Only in Luke 16:22-23 (the rich man and Lazarus). Related imagery: reclining with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom (Matt 8:11, Luke 13:28-29).
78: Abraham's bosom is the place of the righteous dead before the resurrection, separated from the place of torment by a great chasm (Luke 16:26).
80: Jesus uses familiar folk imagery to reverse expectations about wealth and blessing; the story's point is the sufficiency of Moses and the Prophets (Luke 16:31), not afterlife geography.
82: Tertullian located Abraham's bosom within the lower regions, a place of refreshment for faithful souls distinct from heaven, awaiting the resurrection (*Against Marcion* 4.34; *On the Soul* 7 and 55).
84: First, the sky and the cosmos above the earth; second, the dwelling place of God, the realm where his will is fully done. In Jewish idiom 'heaven' could also stand reverently for God himself (e.g. 'kingdom of heaven'). Scripture speaks of heaven as God's throne and of the 'third heaven' (2 Cor 12:2). In the New Testament the believer's hope is stored in heaven and comes from heaven, culminating in heaven and earth united (Rev 21:1-3).
85: Shamayim occurs about 420 times in the Hebrew Bible; ouranos about 270 times in the New Testament (frequently in Matthew, including the phrase 'kingdom of heaven' about 32 times). Heaven is both created (Gen 1:1) and unable to contain God (1 Kgs 8:27). Believers' citizenship is in heaven, from which they await a Saviour who will transform their bodies (Phil 3:20-21).
86: Heaven as final home (popular Western piety)
87: The saved go to heaven at death and remain there forever in the presence of God; resurrection and renewal are often affirmed but receive less emphasis.
88: New creation emphasis (e.g. N. T. Wright, J. Richard Middleton)
89: Heaven is God's dimension of present reality where the inheritance is kept safe; the final hope is not leaving earth for heaven but heaven coming to earth in resurrection and new creation ('life after life after death').
91: Heaven is ultimately the state of communion with God (the beatific vision in Catholic theology; theosis and participation in the divine energies in Orthodox theology), which the souls of the saints enjoy now and which the resurrection will complete bodily.
93: 'Heaven' frequently functions as a reverent substitute for the divine name; 'the kingdom of heaven' means God's reign, not a place above the clouds.
95: Jewish eschatology divided history into 'this age' ('olam ha-zeh), marked by sin, oppression and death, and 'the age to come', when God would set the world right, raise the dead and establish his reign. The New Testament adopts this two-age scheme but claims the age to come has already broken into the present through Jesus' resurrection and the Spirit ('already and not yet').
96: Explicit two-age contrast in Matt 12:32, Mark 10:30, Luke 18:30, Luke 20:34-36, Eph 1:21. Believers have 'tasted the powers of the age to come' (Heb 6:5) and are those 'on whom the ends of the ages have come' (1 Cor 10:11). The rabbinic phrase 'olam ha-ba is prominent in the Mishnah (e.g. m. Sanhedrin 10.1, 'all Israel has a share in the world to come').
98: The age to come has begun with the resurrection of Jesus and the gift of the Spirit, but awaits completion at his return; Christians live in the overlap of the ages.
100: The age to come is chiefly the future era after Christ's return; the present age remains evil (Gal 1:4) until then.
101: 'Olam ha-ba can denote both the messianic age with resurrection and the spiritual world the righteous enter after death; rabbinic sources are not uniform, and Maimonides emphasized its spiritual character.
103: Literally 'pertaining to an age'. In biblical usage it can mean 'everlasting' (of God, Rom 16:26), 'ancient' or 'long-lasting' (the 'eternal' times of Rom 16:25, which have an end), or 'belonging to the age to come'. Its Hebrew counterpart 'olam can mean 'forever' but also 'for a long time' or 'for the duration of a life or order' (e.g. a slave serving 'forever', Exod 21:6).
104: About 70 occurrences in the New Testament, over 40 of them in the phrase 'eternal life' (zōē aiōnios). Also eternal fire (Matt 25:41, Jude 1:7), eternal punishment (Matt 25:46), eternal destruction (2 Thess 1:9), eternal glory, eternal redemption (Heb 9:12) and the eternal God (Rom 16:26). 'Olam occurs over 400 times in the Hebrew Bible. John defines eternal life qualitatively as knowing God (John 17:3).
106: In eschatological contexts aionios means 'without end'. Augustine argued (*City of God* 21.23) that because Matt 25:46 uses the same word for punishment and life, if life is endless, so is punishment.
108: Aionios primarily means 'of the age to come' and need not imply endless duration; 'aionios punishment' can be the corrective chastisement (kolasis) of the coming age. Ilaria Ramelli and David Konstan's study *Terms for Eternity* (2007) is often cited, though its conclusions are disputed.
110: Aionios describes the permanence of a result, not an ongoing process: 'eternal redemption' (Heb 9:12) and 'eternal judgment' (Heb 6:2) are once-for-all acts with everlasting effects, so 'eternal destruction' or 'eternal punishment' can be an irreversible destruction.
112: Especially in John, eternal life is a quality of life, the life of the age to come experienced now through knowing God (John 5:24, John 17:3), not merely endless duration.
114: The final state of the cosmos, in which God renews or recreates heaven and earth, removes death, sin and curse, and dwells with his people. The Greek kainos usually stresses newness of quality rather than an entirely different thing (neos).
115: Isaiah introduces the phrase (Isa 65:17, Isa 66:22) with a picture of long life, building, planting and peace. 2 Pet 3:13 and Rev 21:1 take it up. Paul speaks of creation itself being freed from bondage to decay (Rom 8:19-23); Jesus of the 'regeneration' (palingenesia, Matt 19:28); Peter of 'the restoration of all things' (Acts 3:21).
117: God redeems and transforms this world rather than discarding it, as the resurrected body is continuous with the old (Rom 8:21). 2 Pet 3:10 'will be found' (heurethēsetai, in the best manuscripts) suggests exposure and purification rather than annihilation. Held by Irenaeus, many Reformed and Catholic theologians, and N. T. Wright.
119: The present cosmos will be destroyed by fire and replaced by a wholly new creation (2 Pet 3:10-12, Rev 21:1 'the first heaven and first earth passed away'). Held by some Lutheran orthodox theologians and many popular dispensational writers.
121: Some, especially in the Platonist-influenced strand of tradition, read the language as symbolic of the heavenly, immaterial blessedness of the saints.
123: The raising of the dead to embodied life. In Second Temple Judaism it was a hope for the end of the age (affirmed by Pharisees, denied by Sadducees). The New Testament proclaims that Jesus has been raised bodily as the 'firstfruits', guaranteeing the future resurrection of those who belong to him, with a transformed 'spiritual body' (sōma pneumatikon) fit for the age to come.
124: Anastasis occurs about 42 times in the New Testament. Clear Old Testament anticipations: Isa 26:19, Dan 12:2 (the clearest), with Ezek 37 as national restoration imagery. Paul's fullest treatment is 1 Cor 15. Jesus speaks of a resurrection of life and of judgment (John 5:28-29); Paul before Felix affirms a resurrection of both righteous and unrighteous (Acts 24:15).
126: The same body that died is raised and transformed, made imperishable; the empty tomb shows continuity between old and new body. This is the consistent teaching of the Creeds ('the resurrection of the flesh/body').
128: Some scholars read 1 Cor 15:44 as a body animated by the Spirit, materially continuous but radically transformed; others (a minority) read Paul as envisaging a body of heavenly substance not tied to the corpse.
130: Strands of Christian piety have emphasized the soul's survival and ascent to God so strongly that resurrection becomes an appendix; critics (Oscar Cullmann, N. T. Wright) argue this reverses the New Testament priority.
131: Resurrection of the dead is a core belief (second blessing of the Amidah; m. Sanhedrin 10.1), though interpreted in different ways by later Jewish thinkers.
133: God's reign or kingly rule, more than a territory: God acting as king to defeat evil, vindicate his people and set the world right. Central to Jesus' preaching. It is present in Jesus' ministry (Luke 11:20) and yet future, to come in fullness (Matt 6:10).
134: 'Kingdom of God' occurs about 65 times in the New Testament (mostly Mark and Luke, also Acts and Paul); 'kingdom of heaven' about 32 times, only in Matthew, likely a reverent Jewish circumlocution with the same meaning. Daniel's vision of an everlasting kingdom (Dan 2:44, Dan 7:13-14) is the main Old Testament background.
136: The kingdom arrived in Jesus' person and works and will be consummated at his return (George Eldon Ladd and many others).
138: Jesus expected an imminent, cosmic, future kingdom (Johannes Weiss, Albert Schweitzer); the delay forced the church to reinterpret it.
140: The kingdom has fully come in Jesus' ministry (C. H. Dodd in his early work); future language is largely symbolic.
142: The kingdom is God's rule in hearts or in the church (strands in Augustine and much later piety); critics say this flattens its political and cosmic dimension.
144: The darkness outside a lit banquet hall, image of exclusion from the messianic feast, accompanied by 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' (grief and anger).
145: Three times, all in Matthew: the 'sons of the kingdom' cast out while Gentiles feast with the patriarchs (Matt 8:12), the guest without a wedding garment (Matt 22:13), and the worthless servant (Matt 25:30). 'Weeping and gnashing of teeth' occurs also in Matt 13:42, Matt 13:50, Matt 24:51 and Luke 13:28.
147: Outer darkness is another image for final damnation, emphasizing separation from God's presence, light and fellowship; it complements fire imagery (both cannot be literal at once, pointing to symbolic language).
148: Loss of reward (some Free Grace interpreters)
149: A minority read Matt 22 and 25 as describing believers who lose reward or status in the kingdom, not damnation. Most commentators reject this as reading against the context.
151: Matt 8:12 in particular warns those who assume covenant privilege; the image belongs to Jesus' prophetic critique within Israel, in addition to any final-judgment sense.
153: In Revelation, the final judgment that follows the first (bodily) death and the resurrection, identified with the lake of fire. The phrase also appears in the Aramaic Targums (e.g. Targum on Deut 33:6, Isa 22:14, Jer 51:39), where it denotes final exclusion from the world to come.
154: Four times, all in Revelation: Rev 2:11, Rev 20:6, Rev 20:14, Rev 21:8. Those who overcome and share in the first resurrection are not harmed by it.
156: Death in Scripture means separation; the second death is final and everlasting separation from God, consciously experienced.
157: 'Death' should be taken at face value: the second death is the final cessation of existence, the reverse of resurrection life.
159: The second death is the death of the sinful self in purifying fire, which may itself open onto life; the strongest form of this view is held by a minority.
161: A restoration to a former or proper state. Used in medicine, astronomy (return of stars to their positions) and politics. In Acts 3:21 Peter speaks of the heavens holding Jesus 'until the times of the restoration of all things which God spoke through the prophets'. Later, through Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, the word became the technical term for the final restoration of all rational beings to God (universal salvation).
162: The noun occurs once in the New Testament (Acts 3:21). The verb apokathistēmi is used of Elijah who 'restores all things' (Matt 17:11, Mark 9:12), the disciples' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6), and healings (Mark 3:5). Related universalizing texts: Rom 5:18, 1 Cor 15:22-28, Eph 1:10, Col 1:20, Phil 2:10-11.
163: Restoration promised by the prophets (most commentators)
